h: IIT faculty: 80 per cent upper caste, 2,631 reserved posts empty
dek: Data obtained through RTI shows that in the country's best-known technical institutes, reservation exists on paper, not in the classroom.
body: After the suicide of Sahil Wakode, a second-year Dalit B.Tech student at IIT Bombay, his parents accused a professor of caste harassment. After this, teachers there marched in support of the accused professor. Pranav Jeevan P., who has a PhD from IIT Bombay, asks why a faculty that rallied so quickly for a colleague stayed silent about earlier suicides and discrimination.

To find answers, the writer filed RTI requests with all 23 IITs in September 2026; only 17 replied. According to his data, more than 80 per cent of the teachers in these institutes are upper caste, and at IIT Kharagpur the share is 91 per cent. Most departments do not have a single SC, ST or OBC teacher, not even some humanities departments that teach caste.

There is no shortage of candidates either: more than half of the applications received since 2025 are from reserved categories. The humanities department of IIT Guwahati received 161 OBC and 100 SC applications, but did not hire even one. By the writer's count, 928 upper-caste teachers hold posts beyond the reservation limit, while 2,631 reserved posts lie empty.

Six IITs have no SC/ST cell at all, and where one exists, it is mostly just an email address. According to the writer, the absence of complaints is proof not of an absence of discrimination but of an absence of trust. The UGC recommends one mental health professional for every 500 students, but only 3 of the 17 IITs meet this. Of the 21 suicides mentioned, 11 were of SC, ST or OBC students.

A task force set up by the Supreme Court asked in November 2025 for the empty posts to be filled within three months, but the institutes are largely ignoring this. The writer demands that reserved posts be filled, that SC/ST cells get legal status and funds, and that counsellors understand caste harassment as a structural problem.
nazar: The IITs are the country's richest and most prestigious public institutions, and it is there that the reservation law seems least enforced. Where the law has teeth, as with committees for sexual harassment complaints, the system works; where it does not, caste quietly keeps the door shut. It is easy to turn Sahil Wakode's death into a case of one professor against one family; the real question is about a structure in which a Dalit or Adivasi student does not see a single teacher like themselves in the classroom.

These figures are the writer's own calculation from incomplete RTI replies, and that is a question in itself: why do public institutions not disclose the caste-wise picture of their own faculty? The Ministry of Education should have this data made public every year.
sawal: Why did IIT Guwahati select none of the 261 reserved-category applicants?
ref: RTI
The Right to Information Act, 2005. Under it, any citizen can ask a government body for information.
SC/ST cell
A unit in educational institutions that hears complaints from Dalit and Adivasi students and staff. In most places it has not been given legal powers.
ank: share of upper castes in IIT faculty

h: Sonia's memoir: taunted for staying silent, taunted for speaking
dek: According to Nikhil Sanjay Rekha Adsule, the real point of 'Belonging' is not its secrets but its refusal to let anyone else decide when a woman may speak.
body: For two decades Sonia Gandhi's silence was used as a weapon against her, and she was called a 'remote control'. Now that her memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love' is out, the BJP is calling it a whitewash. According to Nikhil Sanjay Rekha Adsule, a lawyer and senior scholar at IIT Delhi, this double standard says more about patriarchy in Indian politics than about the book.

The writer recalls Gargi of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, whom Yajnavalkya warned that her head would fall off if she asked too many questions. Tradition forgets that Gargi came back and asked again. According to the writer, Sonia did the same. She came in 1968 as a foreign daughter-in-law, was widowed in 1991, and instead of stepping back as custom expected, she stayed at the centre of politics.

In 2004, when there was a chance she would become Prime Minister, a senior opposition leader reportedly said she would shave her head and wear white, the marks of a widow. From the Italian waitress to the Congress widow, her story was always told by others. The writer also notes that in 2010, during the UPA era under her chairpersonship, the Rajya Sabha passed the Women's Reservation Bill.

The writer does not shy away from the contradiction of dynasty. Sonia's politics began with the name of her husband's family, but in his view patriarchy gave her the role of a widow, and what she did from that place was her own. Drawing on the Italian feminists Carla Lonzi and Luisa Muraro and their idea of starting from oneself, he says every memoir is selective, but telling one's own story is the revolutionary part of this book.
The writer's conclusion is that the fault lies not in women's voices but in the rules that decide when a woman may speak and what she may say.
nazar: Sonia Gandhi belongs to a powerful political family and her story is not the story of an ordinary woman; that difference is worth remembering. Even so, the weapons used against her, birthplace, accent, religion and widowhood, are the same ones used against the woman in a village or small town who wants to speak up in the panchayat. The question is not of supporting or opposing the book, but of why both a woman's silence and her voice are punished in public life.
sawal: Why was widowhood made a weapon of political attack?
ref: Gargi
A woman scholar of the Upanishadic age who questioned Yajnavalkya on philosophy in the court of King Janaka. A symbol of women's knowledge and their right to ask questions.
Patriarchy
A social order in which power and decisions stay in the hands of men. A woman's role is decided by custom.

h: Sonia's book directly challenges Modi's Hindutva
dek: According to Sanjay K. Jha, 'Belonging' turns around the old attack on her foreign origin and puts forward a pluralist understanding of India and Hinduism.
body: For years the Sangh Parivar has attacked Sonia Gandhi over her foreign origin. According to political commentator Sanjay K. Jha, her new memoir 'Belonging' turns this very question around and sets out, against Prime Minister Modi, a different understanding of the Indian nation, Hinduism and culture.

In the book Sonia writes that her ideological ground and Modi's are different. Her understanding of India was shaped by her family's public service and the values of freedom and equality, while Modi's was shaped by RSS thinkers. She describes Modi's India as a country where one faith and culture is placed above all others, with hierarchy, discipline and control at its centre. In her view this is a threat to the system that has held such a diverse country together for nearly 80 years.

Jha explains that against the Sangh's narrow understanding of Hinduism, Sonia holds a pluralist faith with room for many paths and for dissent. She cites Mahatma Gandhi's non-violence and his reading of religion, acknowledges the oppression of caste, and reminds readers that reformers challenged it using Hindu ideas themselves.

In the book Sonia alleges that under BJP rule attacks on minorities and Dalits rose sharply, often without punishment. According to her, the corporate media sided with the government against its opponents, dissenters were jailed in false cases, elected state governments were toppled and the Election Commission was made a tool of those in power. She also says she never had a meaningful conversation with Modi and that this hostility is not personal.

According to Jha, the Congress has made these allegations before, but the book sets them out in finer detail. And talk of cultural equality carries more weight coming from a leader who was targeted for her birthplace.
nazar: This piece is more a summary of the book than a critique, and the writer himself was once a Congress spokesperson. Even so, Sonia's charge against the Election Commission comes at a time when young people are on the streets against names being cut in the SIR, and so the book does not remain just a book of memories.

The real test is that writing about pluralism in a book is one thing, and fighting on the ground for the rights of Dalits, Muslims and Adivasis is another. The Congress will also have to account for its own years in power with the same frankness.
sawal: Will the Congress show the same frankness about its own years in power?
ref: Pluralism
The idea that many religions, languages and ways can live together as equals in one society.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision. The Election Commission's drive to rebuild the voter rolls, which faces allegations of names being cut on a large scale.

h: Tamil Nadu's AI book scam: fake authors and false ISBNs in the library
dek: According to Mukund Padmanabhan, crores' worth of AI-written junk books in Coimbatore's Periyar library is a huge failure of oversight.
body: Coimbatore's Rs 300 crore Periyar Arivulagam library is now at the centre of the country's first AI publishing scam. According to Mukund Padmanabhan, professor of philosophy at Krea University and former editor of 'The Hindu', about Rs 20 crore out of a Rs 50 crore budget was spent on more than 60,000 books. Many of these were written by AI, carried fake authors, were full of wrong information, were overpriced and had fake ISBNs.

According to reports, about 2,000 books came from two publishers, Agal Vilakku and Phoenix, which share the same letterbox as their address. The scam was exposed by the writer Perumal Murugan, who was himself on the book committee set up by the DMK government. Chief Minister Vijay's TVK government is accusing the DMK of corruption in the name of Periyar and Tamil, while the DMK says the irregularities began after the change of government in June. The writer finds this argument weak.

Purchases went through committees at four levels: a 137-member recommendation committee, a 13-member selection committee, and two committees of officials for pricing and final approval. The writer asks whether the books got past these committees, or whether the members signed the lists without checking. The irregularities are said to extend to Chennai's Connemara library, Madurai's Kalaignar library and several districts; even a fake book in the name of economist Jean Dreze was bought.

These books mention a Chief Minister who never existed, and a Jain poetry anthology was described as the work of a single poet. The Madras High Court has asked the vigilance department to register an FIR and freeze the accounts of one publisher. The writer hopes the focus will now shift from political accusations to the details of the purchase process.
nazar: A public library is for people who cannot buy books, such as students in small towns and young people preparing for competitive exams. Serving them AI garbage and false history does more harm than the theft of money. That this happened in a library named after Periyar is all the more bitter, because Periyar fought to take reason and knowledge to the poor. In the age of AI, every state will need an open, public method for checking government book purchases.
sawal: Why did a 137-member committee not catch the fake books?
ref: ISBN
International Standard Book Number. A 13-digit number that gives every published book its own identity.
Periyar
E.V. Ramasamy (1879-1973), a social reformer of Tamil Nadu. He led the Self-Respect Movement against caste, superstition and Brahminism.

h: The era of unconditional US support for Israel is fading
dek: After the Iran war and the midterm elections, Washington is moving from backing Israel blindly to backing it after doing the sums.
body: The writer, who is associated with Chatham House, says the relationship between the US and Israel is no longer what it was. Since 1967, almost every US government has backed Israel, even when its policies went against America's own interests. According to the writer, this blind support is now cooling, and the change is visible not only among leaders but among ordinary Americans too.

The biggest sign of this is that on midterm election day Trump announced an end to the roughly four billion dollars in military aid Israel receives every year. The writer guesses the decision had been made earlier, but announcing it may also have been an attempt to stop a Democratic win. After losing the election, Vice President JD Vance blamed Israel for the defeat, which the writer sees as a clever excuse, because the responsibility for trusting Netanyahu's assessment of the Iran war lies with America itself.

The writer lists anger rising from two sides. On one side are progressives who oppose the use of deadly force in Gaza, the occupation and the spread of settlements in the West Bank. On the other is the 'America First' camp, angry about a costly and failed war that, by the US military's estimate, cost 47 billion dollars. Both camps oppose spending on foreign military aid when needs at home have grown.

According to the writer, the three old pillars of support, sympathy after the Holocaust, shared democratic values and the image of a reliable military partner in the region, have all weakened. Israel gets about 70 per cent of its major weapons from the US, so this is not a relationship of equals. The writer concludes that the alliance will not break, but from now on every bit of support will be tied to the condition of shared interests.
nazar: In the past few years India has made its relationship with Israel almost a question of ideology, from arms purchases to surveillance technology. If the US itself, which has been Israel's biggest backer, is now acting on calculation, then it is time for India too to think about how wise it was to give up its old, principled foreign policy on Palestine.

Ordinary people in India are also paying the real price of the Iran war through the prices of oil, gas and fertiliser, and the millions of Indian workers in the Gulf are closest to this instability. Opposing the war is not just a moral question; it is also a question of our livelihoods.
sawal: Will stopping military aid to Israel change anything for Gaza?
ref: Midterm elections
Elections to the US parliament (Congress) held in the middle of a president's term. In November 2026 the Democrats won both houses.
Yossi Mekelberg
An analyst with the Middle East and North Africa programme of Chatham House, a London think tank.

h: Trump's party lost, but the power to start wars is untouched
dek: The Democrats' win should not be a sigh of relief but a chance to rethink American military power and the unchecked powers of the president.
body: According to Brian Garvey, head of Massachusetts Peace Action, the Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterm elections, and won Senate seats even in states where they had not won for decades. People were angry about rising prices, corruption, authoritarian behaviour and the unpopular war launched against Iran. The writer says these are not separate complaints but symptoms of one disease.

After the defeat, people in the Trump government are distancing themselves from the war. Vice President Vance blamed the Iran war for the loss, Trump announced on election day that military aid to Israel would stop, and Republicans seem to be getting ready to make Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth the scapegoat. The writer calls this the double standard of a government that came to power campaigning against wars and then started one itself.

But the writer's real question is what will change when Trump goes. The president still has the power to start a war without clear legal approval, US forces are deployed across the world, and he alone can decide to use nuclear weapons. In 2025 the US spent about 954 billion dollars on its military, and Trump is asking for one and a half trillion dollars for 2027, along with cuts to domestic programmes.

The writer recalls Martin Luther King's 1967 speech in which he called militarism, racism and greed linked to one another, and said the Vietnam war had swallowed the money for the fight against poverty. The Iran war too has made petrol, diesel, groceries, fertiliser and loans all more expensive. The writer demands that the new Congress take back its constitutional right over war and the budget, put a check on nuclear decisions, and protect universities and institutions from political revenge.
nazar: This debate is just as true for India. Here too, in a war-like atmosphere and in the name of 'national security', debate in Parliament is put off and asking questions about the defence budget is made to seem almost like treason. Yet the same money is cut from schools, hospitals and employment schemes.

Garvey's most useful point is that defeating one leader is not enough; the power that becomes dangerous in the hands of any leader must also be bound. In India too, the independence of institutions and Parliament's oversight cannot be left to the result of any one election.
sawal: Will the new US Congress stop the money for the Iran war?
ref: War powers
Under the US Constitution the right to declare war belongs to Congress, but presidents have often taken military action without its approval.
SIPRI
A research institute in Stockholm that collects data on military spending and the arms trade across the world.

h: Only where power can lose do people think
dek: According to a Pakistani writer, the real test of a country is whether the powerful there can lose an election.
body: Faisal Islam answers a question from his readers: what is the opposite of 'a country on trial'? His answer is simple: a healthy system is one in which power can lose and critics can win.

He offers the US as an example. Despite Trump's pressure on universities, the media and judges, voters took both houses of Congress away from his party. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, whom Trump attacked by name and against whom millions of dollars were poured in, reached the Senate. Ilhan Omar won again. In Israel too, in an election held in the middle of a war, Netanyahu fell short of a majority, the Arab parties nearly doubled their seats, and the election commission rejected allegations of rigging.

Speaking of India, the writer says plainly that he does not defend the Modi government's pressure on the media and universities, but in 2024 voters took away the BJP's majority on its own and Modi had to form a coalition. In his view, there student movements are answered by politicians, not by the army.

On Pakistan he does not argue over any particular election; he simply lists the familiar patterns: slow counting at midnight, constituencies redrawn for desired results, and results decided in advance. His argument is that fear kills thinking by punishing it, and staged elections kill it by making it useless. When a vote is not even counted, people stop thinking. Democracy is slow, but it can correct its mistakes, and a system that cannot lose cannot learn either. The writer's first reform is just this: every vote should be counted as it was cast.
nazar: A writer from a neighbouring country is looking at India as a country where power can still lose, and this praise reminds us of our responsibility. In a time of names being cut from voter rolls, questions over the fairness of the Election Commission and shrinking space for the opposition, this trust will not survive on its own.

The writer's most important point is that a vote is a completed thought. For the poor, Dalit, Adivasi and minority citizens who have the least power, the vote is the biggest means of making themselves heard. Protecting it is protecting democracy.
sawal: How much trust is left in India that every vote is counted?
ref: Abdul El-Sayed
A Michigan doctor and progressive politician; according to the writer, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The Friday Times
An old liberal Pakistani magazine from Lahore, now published online.

h: Prayer meeting attacked in Bardhaman, and the victims are the ones detained
dek: After a mob attacked a house church in a village in Purba Bardhaman, the police kept the worshippers, not the attackers, at the police station all night.
body: According to an Alt News report, on the morning of 1 November a Hindutva group of about 40 people attacked a Sunday prayer being held in a house in Rayan village in Purba Bardhaman district. The attackers allegedly accused the pastor and worshippers of conversion and 'honey trap', beat them with bamboo sticks, belts and kicks, and made them shout 'Jai Shri Ram'.

Pastor Chhotu Ruidas says an influential man of the village first slapped him, then the kitchen door was broken and he was dragged out. A 17-year-old boy suffered a deep head wound and an elderly widow's finger was broken. They were allegedly made to do sit-ups while holding their ears.

According to Pastor Jose Bernard, no one came despite several calls to the police station. When the police arrived after a call to 112, they detained 20 women, three minors and eight men. The women were released at 11 pm and the men at 1 am.

Bernard alleges that he gave a written complaint, but the attackers entered the police station, grabbed him by the collar in front of the police, threatened to kill him and made him withdraw the complaint. Station in-charge Debabrata Mukherjee denied the threat and said the complaint was withdrawn voluntarily and that local people had also filed a counter-complaint.
Bernard denies the conversion allegations. Ruidas has not returned to the village out of fear.
nazar: For the past few weeks there have been regular reports of attacks on Christians in Bengal, and the most worrying thing in this case is the conduct of the police, who detained the injured and let the complaint be withdrawn. When even the police station is not safe for a complainant, small minority communities are left with no path to the law.
sawal: Why did the injured worshippers, not the attackers, spend the night at the police station?
ref: House church
A small Christian prayer meeting held in someone's home. In villages without a separate church building, this is the usual way.
Counter-complaint
A complaint filed by the accused side in answer to the victim's complaint. Often used to pressure the victim into a settlement.

h: Old video from Bangladesh, false claim of opposition to Diwali
dek: A speech given during a beef row at Jagannath University in Dhaka was spread in India as a threat to stop Diwali.
body: On 7 November a 25-second clip spread fast on social media, in which a young man says in Bangla that 'Hindutva aggression' or 'Indian aggression' will not be allowed at Jagannath University. It was claimed that Muslim students of this Dhaka university had called Diwali Hindutva aggression and announced a stop to celebrations on campus.

According to Alt News, the clip was posted by an X handle called 'Voice of BD Hindus', which described it as an announcement by Jamaat student leaders, and several well-known Indian users, including Monika Verma, passed it on with the same claim.

The check found that the video had already appeared on 16 October on the Bangladeshi channel Desh Shomoy News. The actual matter concerned a beef feast on campus: on 12 October Hindu students objected to a beef feast near the central temple, on 14 October the administration banned animal slaughter on campus, and the speech was given at a student union press conference the same day.

In a 17-minute live video of that event on Facebook, student union office-bearer Mustafizur Rahman is seen opposing the ban on animal slaughter. Alt News says there was no mention of Diwali anywhere in the event.
On the contrary, this year a Kali Puja pandal was set up on the same campus and students made alpana. Alt News has declared the viral claim false.
nazar: Cutting up a local campus dispute in a neighbouring country and serving it in India as a plot against a festival is a well-known recipe of hate. The target of such clips is not Bangladesh but Muslims here, who are put under suspicion at every festival.
sawal: Why is there no accountability for the big handles that spread false claims?
ref: Reverse image search
A way to find the real and older source of a picture or video frame on the internet. A basic fact-checking technique.

h: Flood of deepfakes and old videos over Arunachal border tension
dek: After reports of an India-China face-off, fake videos of army officers and old clips from other countries were spread as a fresh clash.
body: On 22 October the ITBP chief confirmed a new face-off between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh. According to a BOOM report, within a few days social media was flooded with AI-made videos, old footage and mismatched clips.

The most serious case was deepfakes of senior army officers. One clip showed Lieutenant General Gireesh Kalia 'admitting' that China had occupied some areas of Arunachal, while the real footage was from October 2023 and was about infiltration in Jammu and Kashmir. Fabricated videos also circulated in the names of Lieutenant General Manoj Kumar and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh.
Congress spokesperson Ritu Choudhary shared the Kalia deepfake, after which Union Minister Kiren Rijiju accused the party of damaging the army's image.

On the other side, several old clips circulated with claims sometimes of an Indian defeat and sometimes of local people chasing away Chinese soldiers. These included the 2020 Galwan clash, a 2021 Tawang video, a military exercise in Kazakhstan, a religious fair in Doti in Nepal and even registration for the Amarnath Yatra.

According to BOOM, a video of a clash between security forces and villagers, presented as a crackdown on civilians amid Chinese intrusion, was actually of a protest on 29 September in Beging village against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project. BOOM has so far done seven fact-checks related to Arunachal.
nazar: When there is tension on the border, the truth is the first to lose, and this time the lies came from every side, from supporters of the government and from the opposition too. The biggest loss is to the people of Arunachal, whose pictures of protest against the dam are now getting lost in false stories of national security.
sawal: Why does the government not itself give correct information about the border?
ref: Deepfake
A video or voice made with AI in which a person appears to say what they never said. Most dangerous at times of elections and war.
Siang Upper Project
A very large dam proposed on the Siang river in Arunachal. The local Adi community opposes it for fear of displacement.

h: Bastar's Pedda Korma: the village rejects a returning Maoist leader
dek: The protest against a former Maoist leader who came to the village with the police after surrendering shows that old wounds are still raw even after the war has ended.
body: The Chhattisgarh government declared victory over the Maoists in March 2026. According to this ground report by Scroll, in Pedda Korma, a village of 178 households in Bijapur district, this victory has turned into a new tension.

Dinesh Modiyam and Papa Rao, leaders who surrendered in April, came to the village with police and revenue officials for an event of the government's 'Niyad Nellanar' scheme. Dinesh is now in the District Reserve Guard. According to the report, an elderly man pushed Papa Rao and told both of them to leave the village and never come back.

The villagers complain that for years they gave the Maoists shelter, went to jail for not telling the police where they were, and then the leadership ended the movement without asking them. In May 2025 the Maoists killed three people of the village, including two of Dinesh's brothers and a 13-year-old boy. In December 2025, after another leader, Vella Modiyam, died in an ambush, the police arrested 11 people.

According to the villagers, after Dinesh's surrender the police called 93 people of the panchayat cadres or supporters and told them to surrender, though barely a third of them were armed. Today 19 people from the village are in jail, and many suspect their names were given by Dinesh. The Bijapur SP did not allow a conversation with Dinesh.
Since 2001, 17 people of the village have been killed, several of them in custody. Today about 11 people are in the police or paramilitary forces.
nazar: The government's 'victory' figures do not show the Adivasi villages that were crushed between violence from two sides and are still caught between jail, suspicion and revenge. Real peace will come to Bastar only when a path opens to the release of innocent prisoners and to truth and justice for those who were killed, not just through camps for government schemes.
sawal: What will happen to the cases of Pedda Korma's 19 prisoners?
ref: Niyad Nellanar
A 2024 scheme of the Chhattisgarh government, whose name means 'your good village'. It claims to take government schemes to villages within 5 kilometres of new security camps.
District Reserve Guard
A Chhattisgarh police force that recruits local Adivasis and surrendered Maoists.

h: US embassy post shows India as 'partly free' again
dek: The US embassy in Australia shared a Freedom House map in which India is 'partly free' for the sixth year in a row.
body: According to a Scroll report, the US embassy in Australia posted a world map on X that shows India among the 'partly free' countries. The map is based on 'Freedom in the World', the 2026 annual report of the American organisation Freedom House, which rates political rights and civil liberties in 195 countries and 13 territories on a 100-point scale.

This time India got 62 out of 100, one less than in the previous report. Until 2020 India was in the 'free' category; it was downgraded in 2021 and has been 'partly free' for six years in a row since then.

The report says India is a multi-party democracy, but under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP government, discriminatory policies have grown and the persecution of Muslims has increased. The harassment of journalists, non-governmental organisations and critics of the government has grown considerably, and the BJP is accused of using government institutions against its opponents.
The report also records that Muslims, Dalits and Adivasis are still on the economic and social margins. Freedom House receives money from the US government.
The report carries no response from the Indian government, the BJP, or the US and Australian governments. The Indian government has in the past dismissed such rankings as biased.
nazar: When the embassy of a 'friendly' country itself shares this map, it is no longer easy to brush it off as just a Western conspiracy. More important than the rating is the truth behind it: the space for freedom for journalists, Muslims, Dalits and Adivasis is shrinking year after year.
sawal: Will the government brush off the report as a conspiracy this time too?
ref: Freedom House
A Washington-based non-governmental organisation that each year releases ratings of democracy and civil liberties in countries. It is funded by the US government.

h: Firecrackers outside Kolkata hospitals, court order ignored
dek: On the night of Diwali and Kali Puja, noise and toxic air near hospitals were recorded at several times the set limits.
body: In its order of 29 October, the Supreme Court limited firecrackers to between 8 pm and 10 pm and banned them within 300 metres of sensitive places such as hospitals. According to a Down To Earth report, both these restrictions were openly broken in Kolkata on the night of 8 November.

The environmental group Sabuj Mancha monitored the surroundings of five hospitals. Firecrackers were allegedly burst within 30 metres of the BC Roy children's hospital, medical students set off fireworks on the RG Kar campus, and rockets were fired after midnight at MR Bangur hospital.

Near BC Roy hospital the average noise was 71.3 decibels, against a limit of 50, and the PM 2.5 level reached 340, more than five times the 24-hour standard. Outside the cardiac ICU of RG Kar, PM 2.5 was about six times the standard, and near Ramakrishna Mission Seva Pratishthan about seven times. These are short-duration readings.

According to Central Pollution Control Board data, the AQI in Ballygunge rose from 100 at 10 pm to above 400 by midnight, that is, into the 'severe' category. The state pollution board received 57 complaints during the night, 37 of them after 10 pm.

The report also says that of the state's 251 recognised manufacturers, only six had the board's required no-objection certificate, and according to activists the police were rarely seen on the streets that night.
nazar: When court orders and government restrictions stay on paper, the first to pay the price are the patients and newborns who cannot even complain. The debate on pollution often stays confined to Delhi, while in cities like Kolkata the failure of enforcement is just as deep.
sawal: How many cases were registered against those who burst firecrackers near hospitals?
ref: PM 2.5
Particles of dust and smoke smaller than two and a half microns that reach the lungs and the blood. India's 24-hour standard for it is 60 micrograms per cubic metre.
Silence zone
The area within 100 metres of hospitals, schools and courts where the noise limit is lowest. At night the limit is 40 decibels.

h: Sonam Wangchuk removed from Leh protest site and taken home
dek: Protests grow in Ladakh against holding hill council elections in the bitter cold, and the administration bans sit-ins and rallies.
ask: Put off the elections till March, give Ladakh constitutional safeguards and statehood
body: On Wednesday Ladakh Police removed climate activist Sonam Wangchuk from the protest site in Leh, took him home and advised him to stay indoors. Police say the action was taken under prohibitory orders issued by the Chief Electoral Officer and the Leh District Magistrate. Wangchuk was protesting against the hill council elections along with leaders of the Leh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance.

The dispute is about the timing of the elections. Municipal and panchayat elections are due on 21 November, and elections to eight autonomous hill development councils on 4 December. In this season the temperature drops to as low as 30 degrees below zero. According to MP Haneefa Jan, about 20 percent of the population leaves Ladakh in winter. He has written to the Lieutenant Governor asking for the elections to be held after March.

The Chief Electoral Officer has banned sit-ins, hunger strikes, rallies and every such collective political activity within the municipal limits of Leh and Kargil while the model code of conduct is in force. Wangchuk appealed to several leaders, including the President, the Prime Minister and the Home Minister, to have the elections postponed, and warned of an agitation. He alleges that the administration is rushing the elections, while talks with the Home Ministry on statehood and constitutional safeguards have been stalled since 15 October.
nazar: In a region that has no legislature of its own, the hill council is the people's voice. Holding its elections in a season when one in five people is away, and then banning protest itself, completes the ritual of democracy but not its spirit. Ladakh's demands will be settled through talks, not prohibitory orders.
sawal: How representative can an election held amid snow and seasonal migration be?
ref: Leh Apex Body and KDA
Two fronts of political and religious groups from Leh and Kargil that have campaigned together since 2019 for statehood for Ladakh and for the Sixth Schedule.
LAHDC
Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council: the autonomous councils of Leh and Kargil, which are the main elected bodies of local government since Ladakh has no legislature.

h: Siang dam protest: 18 Pasighat students arrested, union pleads for release before exams
dek: The Jawaharlal Nehru College students' union has asked the SP to free their jailed classmates before the December exams.
ask: Release the arrested students before their exams
body: In Pasighat, Arunachal Pradesh, the Jawaharlal Nehru College students' union has given a memorandum to East Siang Superintendent of Police Pankaj Lamba, seeking the early release of students arrested after protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project. According to the SP, at least 18 students of the college were arrested; 10 of them are still in judicial custody and 8 have been released on bail.

The arrests followed a protest in Pasighat on 23 October. According to the report, the protest turned violent after alleged excesses by security forces. The NHPC office and the police complex were allegedly targeted, police vehicles were damaged, and the homes of several leaders, including local MLAs and the BJP state president, were damaged. Police have registered several cases.

The union says semester exams are in December, and if the custody drags on, both the students' studies and their results will suffer. The union sought release through due legal process and promised to counsel the students to maintain discipline and peace. The 11,200 megawatt project is opposed mainly by people of the Adi community, who fear that their ancestral villages, fields and forests will be submerged.
nazar: The question of a dam on the Siang is a question of the Adi community's land and consent. The violence should be investigated, but keeping the young people of an entire college in jail for months comes close to turning dissent into a crime. If the government wants dialogue, it could begin by letting the students sit their exams.
sawal: Why must students be kept in jail to build consent for a dam?
ref: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project
A proposed 11,200 megawatt project on the Siang river, which the Centre sees as a response to China's Yarlung Tsangpo dam; local Adi villages oppose it over submergence and displacement.

h: No teachers at Sungro school in Wokha: students' union pauses its agitation but does not end it
dek: In Nagaland, a Lotha students' union has halted the second phase because of exams and warned of a third phase over its demand for permanent teachers.
ask: Appoint permanent teachers at Sungro school right away
body: In Nagaland's Wokha district, the Lotha Middle Range Students' Union has for now halted the second phase of its agitation against the shortage of teachers at Government Higher Secondary School, Sungro. The reason is that exams are under way in schools in the area. Earlier, the union had shut government schools in the Middle Range and the SDEO office in Sanis.

The union rejected the outcome of a meeting held on 9 November with the Principal Director of School Education. At the meeting it was agreed to send a temporary political science teacher in place of one on maternity leave, to bring the English teacher back on 10 November, and to provide a graduate teacher in the coming rationalisation of posts. The union considers this inadequate, and also criticised the district and school representatives who accepted the decision.

The union's minimum demands are two more graduate teachers, one Hindi teacher, and a clerk to be sent to the school from the DEO office in Wokha. The union also objected to the Principal Director's alleged remark that he does not recognise civil society organisations. The union said a third phase would begin if its demands are not met soon.
nazar: A school for 153 children from seven villages is running on temporary arrangements, and this is the story of thousands of schools in hill and Adivasi (indigenous) areas. When students have to shut schools to win their right to be taught, that is a failure of the education department, not of the protesters.
sawal: How long will permanent teachers for remote schools exist only on paper?
ref: SDEO
Sub-Divisional Education Officer: the office at sub-division level that oversees government schools and the posting of teachers.

h: Evicted families in Dhubri's Alamganj under the open sky, demand relief and land
dek: After the homes of more than 550 families were demolished in Assam, the local MP has called for a halt to evictions and for alternative land.
ask: Stop the evictions, give the displaced food, shelter and alternative land
body: Dhubri MP Rakibul Hussain has demanded immediate food, shelter and alternative land for the families uprooted by the eviction drive in Alamganj in Assam's Dhubri district. At a press conference in Dhubri on Monday he called the drive inhuman and said poor families, including small children, are spending nights in the open in the cold. He asked the government to stop further evictions.

In the drive, which began on 1 November, about 650 bigha of land has been cleared using more than 50 bulldozers. According to reports, more than four thousand people from over 550 families have been made homeless, most of them Bengali-speaking Muslims, and a mosque and a madrasa have also been demolished. The government calls it the removal of encroachments from government land, and plans an industrial park on the cleared land.

Hussain says landless families should get land under government policy, and alternative arrangements should be made before any eviction. He alleged that the drive is linked to handing land to the Adani Group, though this has not been confirmed. Cases of some affected families are pending in court; the Gauhati High Court has a hearing on 13 November, and a protest is being planned in Delhi on 14 November.
nazar: In an area where many people have already lost their land to river erosion, uprooting families, and in winter at that, looks less like removing encroachments and more like targeting a community. Eviction without rehabilitation goes against the constitutional right to life, whatever paper says the land belongs to the government.
sawal: Where are evicted families to spend the winter without rehabilitation?
ref: Bigha
A unit of land measurement; in Assam one bigha is roughly equal to one third of an acre.
River erosion and displacement
Erosion by the Brahmaputra costs thousands of families in Assam their land every year, and many are forced to settle on government land.

h: Tamil Nadu raises compensation for victims of the Thoothukudi police firing
dek: Families of the 13 people killed in the anti-Sterlite movement will now get a total of Rs 50 lakh each, and the 40 seriously injured Rs 10 lakh each.
body: The Tamil Nadu government has ordered additional relief of Rs 5.25 crore for victims of the 2018 anti-Sterlite protests. According to a government statement, the decision was taken on the direction of Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, after affected families asked for more help.

Each family of the 13 people killed in the police firing had already received Rs 25 lakh; they will now get Rs 25 lakh more, a total of Rs 50 lakh. This will cost Rs 3.25 crore. The 40 seriously injured will be given Rs 5 lakh more on top of the Rs 5 lakh paid earlier, bringing each person's amount to Rs 10 lakh. This will cost Rs 2 crore. The government says the increased compensation was fixed keeping in mind the recommendations of the Aruna Jagadeesan Commission.

On 22 and 23 May 2018, people in Thoothukudi were protesting against Vedanta's Sterlite copper plant over pollution and its effect on health. Police fired on a procession heading towards the Collectorate, killing 13 people. The plant was shut down after this. The report records no new response from families or activists on their demands for accountability.
nazar: Higher compensation after eight years is some relief for the families, and also an admission that their loved ones were wronged. But compensation is no substitute for accountability. Until action is taken against those who ordered the firing, the message will remain that peaceful protest can cost people their lives.
sawal: When will accountability be fixed for those who fired in Thoothukudi?
ref: Aruna Jagadeesan Commission
A one-member commission of a retired Madras High Court judge set up to inquire into the Thoothukudi firing, which raised questions about the role of police and officials.

h: Torsa tea garden sit-in razed, 11 workers arrested
dek: As Adivasi and Gorkha families in Alipurduar face eviction for a land port, a lawyers' group has demanded a halt to the displacement.
body: Adivasi and Gorkha families who have lived for generations in the Torsa tea garden in Alipurduar district, in West Bengal's Dooars region, had been on an indefinite sit-in beside the Asian Highway since 23 July. According to the report, on 2 November two bulldozers and a large police contingent demolished the protest site and arrested 11 people, including four Adivasi women. An Alipurduar court granted them bail on 7 November.

The land is earmarked for the Jaigaon land port project. The Land Port Authority of India asked for 30 acres in 2022, which the state government acquired and sold to the authority. The families say they were never even consulted. They petitioned the district magistrate, the chief minister and local MLAs and proposed an alternative plot, but received no substantive response.

On a complaint by an authority junior engineer, activists Anuradha Talwar, Binay Kerketta and Mahesh Khalkho have been accused of inciting the crowd, though according to the statement they were not at the site. On 6 November the Calcutta High Court said the project may proceed, but anyone removed must be removed through due process of law.
NAJAR, a lawyers' collective linked to the NAPM, has issued a statement demanding a halt to evictions, withdrawal of the cases and compliance with the High Court's order.
nazar: Tea garden workers have lived on this land since colonial times, yet the titles are still not in their names. That weakness was used first to sell the land and then to clear the protest with bulldozers. The High Court has reminded the state that development too must stay within the law. The government now has to engage seriously with the families' proposal for alternative land.
sawal: Who will decide compensation for those evicted without land titles?
ref: Land port
An integrated border checkpost where customs and immigration checks are done on goods and people crossing by road. Jaigaon is on the Bhutan border.
Paschim Banga Cha Majur Samity
A union of North Bengal tea garden workers, which filed a PIL in the Calcutta High Court on behalf of the Torsa families.
ask: No eviction without land, rehabilitation and compensation

h: Canals shut, fields thirsty: Mahoba farmers save their groundnut crop with tankers
dek: It is time to dig up the groundnut in Kamalpur village of Jaitpur block, but the irrigation department has still not released water into the canals.
body: Kamalpur village in Jaitpur block of Mahoba district, Uttar Pradesh, sits these days with its eyes fixed on the canal. According to a Khabar Lahariya report, the farmers' groundnut crop is at the stage where the field needs water before the harvest is dug up, but the irrigation department has not yet released water into the canals.

Farmers say that when the soil is moist, groundnut comes out of the ground easily. Digging in dry, hard ground is heavy going and takes twice the labour. So farmers who cannot wait are finding a way out of their own pockets.

The report says some farmers are paying about Rs 200 a day to hire labourers who carry water and pour it on the fields. Some have ordered a tanker for about Rs 500 and are spreading the water across the field with buckets and lotas (small water pots). In other words, work the canal would have done for free or cheaply now costs cash every day.

Farmers say that if canal water had come on time, this extra spending would have been saved and digging would have been easier. Their complaint is not a fight over rights, only that the department should release water according to the crop calendar.

The report records no response from the irrigation department, nor does it say when the canals will open. This part of Bundelkhand has long suffered drought and low rainfall, and groundnut is a cash crop for many small farmers here. So even a delay of a few days upsets the sums of cost and profit.
nazar: In a government file, canal water is a date, but for a farmer it is the reckoning of the whole crop. When the department follows the office calendar instead of the field calendar, the burden falls on the smallest farmer, who borrows to pay for tankers and labour. In Bundelkhand, the politics of water is decided not by announcements of big dams and schemes but by small delays like this. The irrigation department should make canal timetables public in villages before the crop season.
sawal: Who decides the date for releasing water into Mahoba's canals?
ref: Bundelkhand
A plateau region spread across Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, known for repeated drought, migration and water shortage. Mahoba, Banda and Chitrakoot are among its districts.
Khabar Lahariya
A rural media organisation that began in Bundelkhand and is run by women journalists from Dalit, Adivasi and backward communities.

h: A deadly winter and two teenagers: the fight to save Mongolia's herding tradition
dek: In an Al Jazeera Witness film, two young herders guard their village's horse herd through the deadliest winter on record.
body: In Mongolia's remote Tsakhir valley, horses are not just animals but a means of survival. This film, shown on Al Jazeera's Witness programme on 10 November, is the story of the herders of this valley and an old, risky tradition of theirs.

For generations, when winter came, herders here gathered the whole village's horses into one large herd and handed its care to their bravest young men. These young men stayed with the herd for months, taking it to distant pastures while protecting it from blizzards. The work was also seen as a kind of rite of passage into adulthood.

According to the film's description, the tradition broke off suddenly in 2019 because of growing environmental pressures, and there was fear that the rite would end for ever. The village elders decided that the winter herd would be formed again, and the responsibility was given to two teenage friends.

As it happened, this turned out to be the winter regarded as the deadliest in Mongolia's recorded history. In the dzud of 2023-24, a mix of severe cold, heavy snow and a crust of ice over the ground, more than seven million animals died across the country and thousands of herding families were ruined.

For many hard months the two boys struggle with blizzards, exhaustion and their own inner doubts. The heart of the film is that in such a winter no one survives alone; survival is possible only together.

The film is based on the work of Australian filmmaker Kasimir Burgess, whose feature documentary 'Iron Winter' was shown in competition at Switzerland's Visions du Reel festival in 2025. At the centre of that film are two young herders named Batbold and Tsagaana, and according to those familiar with it, it also records the change in the valley as the new generation is drawn to the cities for work.
nazar: Mongolia's dzud and the hardships of herders in our own Himalayas, Thar or Kutch are parts of the same story: the climate crisis hits first those who did the least to cause it. In India too, nomadic communities such as the Rabari, Gaddi, Bakarwal and Van Gujjar are fighting to save their way of life amid changing weather, shrinking pastures and official indifference. This film is a reminder that traditional knowledge is not backwardness but a training in staying together through hard seasons, and protecting it should be part of climate policy.
sawal: Is there any place for nomadic herders in India's climate policy?
ref: Dzud
A Mongolian disaster in which a summer drought is followed by bitter cold and snow that cover the fodder, and animals die in large numbers from hunger and cold.
Otor
A Mongolian herding tradition of moving herds by season to better, distant pastures so that the grass near home is saved.

h: A village on the banks of the Sindoori, without any romance
dek: Durgesh Kumar Sajal's review of Shirish Khare's story collection 'Nadi Sindoori' says these stories look at the village not as a postcard but as a question.
body: Durgesh Kumar Sajal, a researcher at Dr. Harisingh Gour University in Sagar, reads the thirteen rural stories of Shirish Khare's collection 'Nadi Sindoori' (The River Sindoori) and sees the river as the living memory of a region. The Sindoori is a tributary of the Narmada that flows near Madanpur, and according to the reviewer the whole village moves along with it in these stories.

The review's first big point is about language. The characters' Bundeli is not decoration; it carries the memory of caste, class and community. According to the writer, turning it into standard Hindi would have taken away the stories' social force. The river here is both a livelihood and a threat of death, and the local understanding of its flow becomes a kind of folk geography.

The reviewer finds the question of women and social control in several stories. Love affairs become the place where village morality, caste and power collide. Women are almost absent from cultural events like the Ramlila, and a widow's suicide becomes a comment on a structure that identifies a woman only through a man.

Caste humiliation shows up in small everyday acts, but the review stresses that Khare's Dalit characters are not mere victims; they also answer back. Theft in poverty is shown more as the result of shrinking options than as personal failing, and there is satire on popular faith too, where a petty thief is taken for a saint after an idol is found.

Sajal concludes that this regional writing does not sigh for the past; it is critical. The village's yesterday was no golden age; it was already full of caste and gender inequality, poverty and fear. So the collection becomes a record of experiences that big histories often leave out.
nazar: Writing about the village in Hindi often turns into either lament or romantic nostalgia. If the reviewer is right, 'Nadi Sindoori' takes the third path that is needed more today: Bundelkhand's Dalits, women and jobless young men are not objects of sympathy here but people speaking in their own language. At a time when news of dams on rivers, sand mining and displacement is common, seeing a river as the memory and livelihood of the settlements on its banks is also political work for literature.
sawal: Does turning a dialect into standard Hindi rob it of its strength?
ref: Sindoori river
According to the review, a tributary of the Narmada that flows near Madanpur in the Sagar region of Madhya Pradesh.
Aanchalik katha (regional fiction)
Fiction that centres the dialect, customs and life of a particular region. Phanishwarnath Renu's 'Maila Aanchal' (The Soiled Border) is an example.

h: Trying to see Kalidas as a man, not an idol
dek: Ashutosh Kumar Pandey's review of Yugal Joshi's novel 'Kaho Kalidas!' counts its strengths as well as its weaknesses.
body: Everyone knows Kalidas's poetry, but almost nothing about his life is certain. Historians do not agree on his birth, his era or his court. According to Ashutosh Kumar Pandey, Yugal Joshi's novel 'Kaho Kalidas!' (Speak, Kalidas!) (Manjul) steps into this empty space. It does not claim to be a biography; instead it imagines the man who gave words to love, nature and separation.

The reviewer places it in the tradition of Mohan Rakesh's play 'Ashadh Ka Ek Din' (A Day in Ashadh), where the poet is caught between love, ambition and royal patronage. Joshi adds bodily desire, beauty and an inner search. In the novel Kalidas is first a herdsman named Mihir, whose love Mohini chooses someone else, and from here he learns the difference between seeing beauty and possessing it.

The book is built around six of Kalidas's works, each linked to a stage of his life. The court section is about the clash between honour and creative freedom, and according to the reviewer Joshi takes this crisis beyond a personal dilemma and turns it into a spiritual question. He finds the 'Meghaduta' (The Cloud Messenger) section the most powerful, where it is left open whether the one weeping is the yaksha or the poet himself.

Along with praise, the review lists flaws. The relationship of Mihir and Mohini slips into sentimentality in places, the first half lingers long on love and nature while the court section is wrapped up quickly, and the six-work structure sometimes breaks the pace of the story. The agency and choices of the women characters are praised, but the reviewer makes clear that this is imagination, not historical evidence.
In the end he says it should not be judged as a historical document. The novel's real success is that it urges the reader to go back to Kalidas's original poetry.
nazar: Today, when ancient poets and texts are often presented as idols of national pride, seeing Kalidas as a man who loves, loses and struggles with royal patronage is in itself a necessary dissent. The question of the court and creative freedom has not grown old; today's writer makes the same choice between power, awards and the market. The honesty of the review is also worth noting: it does not shy away from naming flaws along with praise.
sawal: Can a poet keep his own voice while living on royal patronage?
ref: Ashadh Ka Ek Din
Mohan Rakesh's 1958 play, about the conflict of love and ambition between Kalidas, Mallika and the royal court.
Meghaduta
Kalidas's poem in which an exiled yaksha sends a message through a cloud to his beloved in Alaka.
photo_note: Shakuntala lost in thought, Raja Ravi Varma

h: Kakshivan, son of a maidservant, and the insistence on Brahmin birth
dek: Kushagra Aniket's long research essay challenges Karpatri ji's claim that the Vedic sage Kakshivan was a Brahmin by birth.
body: Kushagra Aniket's essay in Samalochan reopens an old debate: into which lineage was the Vedic sage Kakshivan born? The writer argues that he was not born into a high caste, and that the Brahmin status he gained came through tapas (austerity). The essay argues directly with Karpatri ji, who had described Kakshivan as a Brahmin by birth.

According to the story in the Puranas and the Mahabharata, Kakshivan was the son of the sage Dirghatamas and a Shudra maidservant named Ushij. King Bali wanted to send his queen to the blind sage to have a child, but the queen sent the maidservant in her place. According to the writer, Kakshivan later gained Brahmin status through austerities at Girivraja, and the references to him in the Rigveda match this story.

The essay also cites the Dharmashastras, according to which the child of a Brahmin father and a Shudra mother is not considered a Brahmin. The writer offers the example of Vidura, who was likewise the son of a sage and a maidservant and was counted as a Shudra in the tradition.

The sharpest part is the examination of Karpatri ji's evidence. The writer alleges that Karpatri ji took a great deal from an old Hindi book by Dinanath Shastri Saraswat without mentioning it, and that the verse he quoted about a wife named Pradveshi is not found in the Sahyadri Khanda at all. The writer also rejects, one by one, other arguments such as there being two different Kakshivans, the spelling of the name, and the interpretation of the Rigvedic word 'vipra'.

The essay's larger complaint is that traditionalists worry more about the birth of the sages than about their teachings, and do not hesitate to alter texts or hide inconvenient evidence for this. For the writer it is a question of protecting historical truth: a sage's greatness comes from austerity, not caste.
nazar: This is not just a scholars' debate. When caste hierarchy is justified in the name of the scriptures, showing that within the tradition itself there were sages born of maidservants, and that there were later attempts to cover up their birth, strikes at the root of that claim. Essays like this show that the fight with tradition can also be fought by reading tradition's own texts, and this work should be done much more in Hindi.
sawal: Who needs to hide the birth of the sages?
ref: Karpatri ji
Swami Karpatri (1907-1982), a traditionalist ascetic and writer who also founded a party called the Ram Rajya Parishad.
Kakshivan
A sage linked to some hymns of the Rigveda, described in the Puranas as the son of Dirghatamas and the maidservant Ushij.
photo_note: A page from the Valmiki Ramayana, Zainul Abidin

h: Booker winner M. John Harrison: the walls between genres should fall
dek: A long 2003 conversation with Harrison, winner of the 2026 Booker, in Anurag Ankur's Hindi translation, in Samalochan.
body: After M. John Harrison's novel 'The End of Everything' won the 2026 Booker, Samalochan has published in Hindi an old conversation with him by Cheryl Morgan. The conversation appeared in 2003 in the online magazine 'Strange Horizons', and the translation is by Anurag Ankur.

The conversation begins with the 'New Wave' science fiction of the 1960s and 70s, when Harrison was associated with the magazine 'New Worlds' along with writers like Michael Moorcock. In his view this current forced a genre that shied away from sex and politics to grapple with both, and its influence was felt more on the mainstream British novel than on science fiction.

On his 'Viriconium' series he says he lost faith in the nostalgic feeling of his early writing, because time past truly does not return. He wrote the later stories in the shadow of the confused, suspicious Britain of the Thatcher years.

Talking about his middle novels, Harrison describes his characters as driven by desires that are never fulfilled. He sees escapist reading as a politically barren habit, and criticises the belief of Western consumerism that whatever you want is your right. In his view this very thinking produces environmental destruction and inequality. He sees the novel 'Light' as more hopeful.

Harrison says good and evil should not be explained to the reader; the reader should find meaning for themselves, and he learnt this style of only hinting from Katherine Mansfield. Finally he rejects the idea that the walls between genres should be guarded. For him every story is just a story, and these walls will one day fall.
nazar: In Hindi, science fiction and 'fantasy' are still often treated as light stuff. Harrison's point, that escapist writing is politically barren but imaginative genres can take up serious politics and environmental concern, is useful for that debate here. A country struggling with inequality and the climate crisis needs imagination that does not only entertain but also asks questions.
sawal: Will science fiction in Hindi ever be treated as serious literature?
ref: New Wave
A science fiction current of the 1960s and 70s that put psychology, sex, politics and experiments in style ahead of technology.
Booker Prize
Britain's prestigious annual literary prize for a novel published in English.

h: The corporate labourer's Diwali: bonuses, reels and the end of rebellion
dek: In Hindwi's column 'Reel Rasacharya' (The Reel Connoisseur), Rachit laughs at the Diwali of young office workers while making a bitter point.
body: Rachit's satire begins with the reels young office workers made in Diwali week. One complains that a bonus of a few hundred rupees does not even cover the expensive kurta bought for the office party, one celebrates a meagre bonus with theatrical joy, and one dreams of carrying off the office chairs and desks for not getting a bonus at all.

Then the writer asks who these people are. They jokingly call themselves 'corporate labourers'. According to the writer, many of them once wanted to become something else, spent years preparing for competitive exams in places like Delhi's Mukherjee Nagar, and then settled into some company in Noida, Gurugram or Bengaluru. The promise of quitting the job one day is their last comfort.
One sharp observation of the writer is that in our society respect belongs to a handful of posts, such as MP, MLA, DM or SDM. Everyone else just works 'at some company'.

Then comes a fictional story. Abhinav from Patna comes to Delhi to take the civil services exam, sees the weekend life of the IT districts, and leaving behind the long line of paper leaks and failures, takes a job there. Five years later his small rebellions at the office, unscrewing chairs and pocketing spoons, lead to a warning, but when a manager breaks down, that same warning turns into a promotion.

Abhinav forgives everyone, even his own revolutionary ideals, and vows to work hard. The title's nod to Agyeya's famous poem points to this very irony: the rebel's last act is not protest but an application for a place in the line.
nazar: Behind the laughter, this piece gives a true picture of the job market: young people broken by paper leaks, meagre bonuses and no union. Calling oneself a 'corporate labourer' is a joke, but hidden in that joke is an admission that office work is wage labour too. The question is whether this identity will ever turn into an organised demand, or whether the anger will be used up in reels and small pranks.
sawal: Why don't employees who call themselves labourers organise?
ref: Yah Deep Akela
'Yah Deep Akela' (This Lone Lamp), Agyeya's famous poem about bringing a lone lamp into the row. It is a much-discussed Hindi poem on the relationship between the individual and society.
Mukherjee Nagar
An area of north-west Delhi known for thousands of students preparing for the civil services and for coaching institutes.
photo_note: Terrible News, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: Travel was not a holiday, it was a restlessness to survive
dek: This essay from Hari Karki's column 'Ghaam-Paani' (Sun and Rain) moves through the history of travel to show that journeying is also a practice in understanding others.
body: Hari Karki's essay takes the reader to 1453, when the Ottoman armies' conquest of Constantinople closed the overland trade route and European sailors set out to find new sea routes. The writer asks whether a person standing before an unknown sea would feel thrill or fear, and says the desire to travel begins with this very pull.

In his view, travel was not at first a holiday or entertainment. Early humans kept crossing continents in search of food, water and safety, and thousands of years ago reached as far as Australia with very simple means. The writer calls this an inherited restlessness.

Speaking of fear, he calls misleading the common tale that medieval Europeans believed the earth was flat. The real fear was not of falling off the edge of the world but of being cut off from the known world. He also says the 'discovery' of America was not really a discovery, because people already lived there, and an empty space on the map is often the limit of the one looking, not the emptiness of the world.

Along the Silk Road, languages, ideas, skills and stories travelled with goods. The accounts of travellers like Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Xuanzang and Faxian are a precious memory of those societies. According to the writer, travel can break prejudice, but only when the traveller tries to listen to and understand others' food, families and speech instead of judging them.

On the link between walking and thinking, he recalls the journeys of Gandhi, Vinoba Bhave and Martin Luther King, and holds that delay, illness and fatigue are also part of the journey. Finally, drawing on Odysseus's return to Ithaca, he says distance teaches us to understand our own home better.
nazar: Today travel often means taking pictures for social media, and unchecked tourism in the hills becomes a burden on local lives. Karki's reminder that travel is really a practice in listening to others is needed. It is also worth remembering that even today crores of Indian migrant workers travel not for pleasure but out of the same old compulsion the essay speaks of at its start.
sawal: Does today's tourism teach us to listen to others?
ref: Silk Road
A network of old trade routes stretching from China to the Mediterranean, along which religion, language and ideas travelled along with silk.
Xuanzang
A seventh-century Chinese Buddhist monk who made a long journey through India and wrote an account of studying at Nalanda.
photo_note: A bullock cart in the Deccan, around 1850

h: Jaunpur: earthmovers at fields near ethanol plant, farmers allege land grab
dek: Farmers of Gairwah village say a JCB is being run at night on their registered ancestral land and green trees are being cut; the area MLA has asked revenue officials for a time-bound inquiry.
body: A land dispute has broken out over fields next to an ethanol plant in Gairwah village of the Suithakala area in Jaunpur district, Uttar Pradesh. Farmers say the plant management is trying to grab their ancestral, registered land by force and is having the green trees there cut down.

According to the Amar Ujala report, farmers allege that a JCB is being used in the dark of night to change the shape of the land and seize it. After the complaint, the local MLA, Ramesh Singh, reached the spot and heard the farmers out.

The farmers told the MLA that the disputed land is ancestral and registered in their names, yet trees are being felled and soil removed to alter the plot. Revenue department officials were also present at the site.

The MLA directed the revenue officials to hold a fair inquiry and settle the matter within a fixed time. The report does not carry the plant management's version, nor does it make clear in whose name the land is recorded. For now this is the farmers' allegation, and it needs to be investigated.
nazar: In a village, a land dispute usually gets stuck between the paper and the possession. A farmer may hold the sale deed, but if he must guard his field every night to protect it, that is the real weakness. A JCB moving at night, with officials standing by, shows the matter is not only between two parties but about how clear the revenue records are. The inquiry should establish what the land documents say and how the land for the plant was marked out.
sawal: If the land is registered to the farmers, on whose instructions does the JCB move at night?
ref: Sale deed
The registered document of a land sale; in a village it is treated as the strongest proof of ownership.
Khata-khatauni
Revenue department records that list the owner of a plot and its area; after a sale, the name must be entered in them.

h: Four goats in Sonbhadra: an income without selling the land
dek: Regenerate India is testing a model with the aim of reaching nearly 4,000 households across 30 villages, in which four goats per family supply milk, fodder and young animals sold inside the village network.
body: A quiet experiment is under way in the villages of Sonbhadra district, Uttar Pradesh: families are being encouraged to keep four goats alongside their crops, so that they have a second source of income without selling their land. Mukesh Panika of Regenerate India writes in Village Square that the aim is to reach nearly 4,000 households across 30 villages, home to about 28,000 people.

Panika recounts that when he returned to Sonbhadra after the pandemic, several people offered to buy farmland for real estate. The question that began to trouble him was why a rural family should sell its most valuable asset and hand someone else the chance to earn from it, when it could earn from the land itself.

That thinking led to a Farmer Producer Organisation, which began with a handful of families and now includes more than 350 farming households. Panika calls the farmers partners, not 'beneficiaries', because the land, the experience and the generational knowledge are theirs, and so is the right to decide what development should look like.

In the model, each household keeps four goats along with crops and fodder; milk, fodder and young animals are sold through a local network inside the village, and the young are redistributed among other families so that the money circulates within the community. The focus, the writer says, is the Jamnapari breed, known as the 'queen of goats', whose milk can be turned into cheese, ghee and powder.

The piece itself concedes that the model is still being built, that early results are encouraging but the larger goal is not yet met. This is not a report of a scheme's success but an account of an attempt, and it should be read that way, since the writer runs the initiative himself.
nazar: The goat is usually seen as the animal of the poor, yet its milk, its fodder and its young all have a market, and the risk for a small family is lower: one goat dying does not mean selling the whole field. Sonbhadra's experiment is betting on the strength of that small scale. The question is how hard it is to keep a market for milk and fodder alive inside the village, and whether incomes really rise or only the arithmetic of debt changes.
sawal: Can a village build an income without selling its land?
ref: Jamnapari
A well-known Indian goat breed called the 'queen of goats'; it is large-bodied and gives more milk.
FPO
Farmer Producer Organisation, a collective enterprise of farmers that helps with buying, selling and market access.
